scenario: AITA for canceling a family road trip? | My husband and I made plans a few weeks ago to take our toddler on a six-hour road trip to visit some good friends in a scenic part of the country. We planned to leave on Friday morning. This is why I canceled the trip: My husband's car is 15 years old and has 265k miles on it. (He's said repeatedly that he wants to hit 300k.) The check engine and brake lights have been on for several months. A few weeks ago, the car overheated and died while I was driving it, and he discovered a crack in the radiator that he sealed with some kind of epoxy. (He previously said that it probably just needed fluid.) Then the brakes started grinding, and after a few days he agreed to take it into the shop. In the interim, the brakes failed to catch correctly while I was driving our daughter home from daycare, and I narrowly avoided an accident. He had the brakes replaced (although previously he'd said, as with the radiator, that they only needed fluid). Now the check engine light is flashing, and the car is shaking at speeds above 50mph. Every Google search result says this indicates a misfire that could result in catastrophic engine damage (something about the catalytic converter). My husband says he's narrowed it down to a fuel injector problem, and he wants to repair it himself today and go on the road trip tomorrow as planned. I told him that I didn't trust the car and didn't want our daughter in it, and I texted our friends last night and said we couldn't go. Now my husband is angry--he thinks I'm being anxious for no reason because he knows cars better than I do and has done "hundreds of hours of research" into car repair. (He is not a mechanic, but he is very handy, and he's made successful car repairs in the past.) Our friends are disappointed because they planned a weekend of activities that they won't be able to reschedule for several months. No one seems to agree with me that driving would have been unsafe. Am I the asshole?

My husband and I planned a six-hour road trip with our toddler to visit friends in a scenic area. We were supposed to leave on Friday morning. Then the brakes started grinding, and after a few days, he agreed to take it to the shop. In the meantime, the brakes failed to catch correctly while I was driving our daughter home from daycare, and I narrowly avoided an accident. He had the brakes replaced, but he initially thought they only needed fluid. Now the check engine light is flashing, and the car is shaking at speeds above 50 mph. Google searches say this indicates a misfire that could cause catastrophic engine damage, possibly involving the catalytic converter. My husband thinks it's a fuel injector problem and wants to fix it himself today so we can go on the trip tomorrow as planned. I told him I didn't trust the car and didn't want our daughter in it, so I texted our friends last night and canceled. Now my husband is angry, thinking I'm being anxious for no reason because he knows cars better than me and has done a lot of research. Our friends are disappointed because they planned activities they can't reschedule for months. No one seems to agree with me that driving would have been unsafe. Am I the asshole? First, I need to consider the safety aspects. The car has had multiple issues: overheating, radiator crack, grinding brakes that almost caused an accident, and now a misfire causing shaking. These are serious mechanical problems that could lead to accidents or engine failure. As a parent, my priority is the safety of my child. Canceling the trip to avoid potential danger seems reasonable. However, my husband is upset because he believes he can fix the car and that I'm overreacting. He's done successful repairs before, but he's not a professional mechanic. The fact that he's had to fix multiple issues in a short time might indicate that the car is unreliable. The misfire issue is particularly concerning because it can lead to engine damage and potential loss of control while driving. I also need to think about the impact on our friends. They were looking forward to the trip and had planned activities that can't be rescheduled. Canceling might have caused disappointment, but safety should come first. It's possible that they would rather have us safe and sound than attend the planned activities. On the other hand, maybe I could have communicated better with my husband about my concerns. Perhaps finding a middle ground, like getting a second opinion from a professional mechanic or considering alternative transportation, could have been an option. But given the time constraints and the urgency of the issues, that might not have been feasible. In the end, my decision was based on safety, which is a valid concern, especially with a toddler involved. While it's unfortunate that the trip had to be canceled, prioritizing safety is not being the asshole. It's being responsible.
